title: Reading Execution Plans
description: Use SQL Server's execution plans to diagnose slow queries, distinguish table scans from index seeks, and understand the query optimizer's choices.

data.text: Even a correct query can be painfully slow if SQL Server chooses a poor execution strategy. The execution plan tells you what the query optimizer decided to do — and why. Learning to read it is the first step to query optimization.
Before executing a query, SQL Server's query optimizer creates an *execution plan* — a step-by-step recipe of how to retrieve the data. SSMS can display two flavors:

rows: What the optimizer *plans* to do (no execution)

data.title: How to see a plan
data.text: In SSMS, click the 'Include Actual Execution Plan' button (Ctrl+M) or 'Display Estimated Execution Plan' button (Ctrl+L), then run your query. The plan opens in a separate tab at the bottom.
Reading the plan: the flow of data

Execution plans are read right-to-left and top-to-bottom. Each box is an operation (like a table scan or index seek). Arrows show data flow: the width of an arrow represents how many rows are moving between operations — thicker means more rows.

data.caption: Read execution plans right-to-left: data flows from the rightmost (deepest) operation to the leftmost (output)

data.text: The two most common operations you will see:

rows: Reads every row in the table
No suitable index exists, or the table is very small
Uses an index to jump directly to matching rows
A suitable index exists for the WHERE filter

data.title: A query that scans, then one that seeks
The 80/20 rule of table scans
data.text: A table scan is not always bad. If your table has 10 rows, scanning is faster than maintaining an index. SQL Server switches to scans on small tables or when a query returns a large percentage of rows (e.g., 50%+) — an index seek wouldn't help there.
Common expensive operations to watch for

items: Key Lookup / RID Lookup — the optimizer found a row via index but had to go back to the base table for more columns; fix by adding INCLUDE columns to the index
Nested Loops — good for small result sets, but degrades with large data; consider Hash Match or Merge Join
Sort — expensive, especially on large sets; try to avoid by ordering data in the index itself
Cursor — row-by-row processing; almost always a sign that a set-based rewrite would be faster

items.text: Is the query filtering on an indexed column?
items.hint: Add an index on the WHERE / JOIN columns if missing

items.text: Are you using SELECT * when you only need a few columns?
items.hint: List only the columns you need to reduce I/O

items.text: Is there a Key Lookup in the plan?
items.hint: Add INCLUDE columns to cover the extra columns

items.text: Are you using functions on indexed columns in WHERE?
items.hint: Functions on columns make indexes unusable — filter on the raw column instead

data.title: Plan reading essentials
points: Right-to-left: data flows from the deepest operation to the output
Thick arrows = lots of rows; thin = few — look for bottlenecks where many rows get reduced
Table scans are OK on small tables but a red flag on large ones
Index Seek is the goal for filtered queries; Key Lookups suggest adding INCLUDE columns
Estimated plan = what the optimizer thinks; Actual plan = what really happened
